title: Osimertinib Plus Platinum-based Chemotherapy in Patients With EGFR-Mutated Advanced NSCLC Post-progression on First-Line Osimertinib: ORCHARD.
authors: Goldman JW, Riess JW, Cho BC et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: ORCHARD (NCT03944772) was a biomarker-directed, phase II, platform study conducted to characterize resistance mechanisms and evaluate novel treatment combinations in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) following progression on first-line osimertinib. We report results from the module evaluating osimertinib plus platinum-based chemotherapy.
METHODS: Patients received osimertinib (80 mg once daily) plus ≤ 4 cycles of platinum-based doublet chemotherapy (pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 plus carboplatin AUC5) on day 1 of every 21-day cycle, followed by pemetrexed maintenance until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or another discontinuation criterion. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1. Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DoR), overall survival (OS), and safety.
RESULTS: Thirty-one patients received study treatment. Eight patients had a confirmed partial response (ORR 26%; 80% CI, 16-39). Median DoR was 7.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-not calculable). Median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 4.0-7.5); PFS events were reported in 29 (94%) patients. Median OS was 10.9 months (95% CI, 8.5-15.0); 20 (65%) patients had died at data cut-off. Grade ≥ 3 adverse events (AEs) occurred in 20 (65%) patients; AEs leading to discontinuation of any treatment occurred in 7 (23%) patients.
CONCLUSION: In patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC who had progressed on first-line osimertinib, osimertinib plus platinum-based chemotherapy demonstrated a modest clinical benefit and manageable safety profile, consistent with the individual drug profiles.

title: Role of maintaining the TKI backbone in oncogene-driven NSCLC after progression.
authors: Piazza F, Sharma R, Esposito A et al.
abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have marked a turning point in the treatment of oncogene-addicted non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), offering unprecedented efficacy. Yet, most tumors eventually develop resistance and progress, often prompting discontinuation of the targeted agent and a switch to non-targeted therapies such as chemotherapy. We explored current evidence on maintaining inhibition of the oncogenic driver beyond progression in a narrative literature review through August 24, 2026, including clinical trials, retrospective analyses, case reports, case series, and preclinical models. Among all drivers, only EGFR-mutated NSCLC provided phase II/III evidence supporting maintenance of driver inhibition beyond progression. Combinations of EGFR-directed therapies with chemotherapy or MET inhibitors were associated with improved response rates and progression-free survival (PFS) compared with chemotherapy or MET inhibitor monotherapy, although these trials had several limitations. ALK and KRAS G12C evidence was limited to early-phase trials with small cohorts and modest clinical signals, while the remaining drivers (RET, METex14, NTRK, HER2, ROS1, BRAF, and EGFR exon 20) evidence was largely preclinical or anecdotal, making continuation experimental. Co-occurring resistance mechanisms, heterogeneous tumor evolution, and potential additive toxicity complicate interpretation of the backbone's contribution to clinical benefit. Continuation should therefore not be applied routinely but tailored to the pattern and site of progression, re-biopsy findings, CNS disease control, expected toxicity, and patient preferences. Given the rarity of many oncogenic drivers and the challenges of conducting adequately powered randomized trials, definitive data may remain available for several resistance scenarios.

title: Biomarker-guided targeted therapy in lung adenocarcinoma: A concise review of precision oncology advances, resistance mechanisms, and emerging strategies.
authors: Mall T, Bachhar V, Joshi V et al.
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), a major subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality despite major therapeutic advances. Precision oncology has revolutionized the management of LUAD by identifying actionable molecular biomarkers and developing targeted therapies. In this review, we summarize the major predictive biomarkers in LUAD, including EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, MET, RET, BRAF, HER2, NTRK, and PD-L1, and describe the currently approved targeted therapies and emerging therapeutic strategies. Recent advances in selective inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, and immune checkpoint inhibitors that have improved clinical outcomes in molecularly defined patient populations are highlighted. The review also discusses the molecular basis of acquired resistance, such as on-target mutations, bypass signalling activation, histological transformation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition that continue to limit long-term therapeutic efficacy. We also discuss emerging strategies to overcome resistance, including combination therapies, next-generation inhibitors, liquid biopsy-guided monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted precision medicine. Collectively, these findings highlight the need for comprehensive molecular characterization and integrated biomarker-guided treatment strategies to improve therapeutic decision-making and clinical outcomes in LUAD.

title: Development of Potent and Selective EGFR-PROTACs Based on Macrocyclic Fourth-Generation EGFR Inhibitors.
authors: He Q, Cheng Y, Zhang Q et al.
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutant-driven non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) frequently develops acquired resistance to third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), particularly through the EGFR C797S mutation. Existing EGFR-targeting proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) remain limited by unfavorable pharmacokinetics and suboptimal selectivity inherited from their parent TKIs. To address these limitations, we developed HQY1480, a next-generation PROTAC derived from the macrocyclic fourth-generation EGFR inhibitor BI-4020. Systematic linker and E3 ligase ligand optimization enabled potent and selective degradation of multiple clinically relevant EGFR mutants with single-digit nanomolar DC50 values. HQY1480 exhibited favorable pharmacokinetics, stronger suppression of oncogenic signaling than BI-4020, and no detectable off-target degradation in proteomic profiling. In xenograft models, HQY1480 outperformed BI-4020, overcame osimertinib resistance, and effectively inhibited tumor growth at low doses, while inducing robust EGFR degradation in patient-derived xenografts. These findings establish HQY1480 as an effective and well-tolerated lead PROTAC for EGFR-mutant NSCLC with acquired resistance to third-generation TKIs.

title: Molecular, histopathological, and clinical risk factors for overall metastatic disease and brain metastases in surgically resected stage I-III lung cancer.
authors: Dyrbekk APH, Suhrke P, Ludahl MO et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, including among patients diagnosed with potentially curable disease. Current decisions regarding perioperative treatment and follow-up rely on a limited number of established prognostic factors. Further knowledge is needed regarding the clinical, histopathological, and molecular factors associated with subsequent metastatic disease, particularly brain metastasis (BM), which is associated with poor prognosis. We investigated these factors in a large cohort of patients with surgically resected stage I-III lung cancer followed for more than five years. BM was associated with higher pathological tumour and lymph-node stage and younger age at surgery. Lung adenocarcinoma was associated with a higher risk of BM than lung squamous cell carcinoma. Several molecular alterations were associated with metastatic disease or BM, including KRAS mutations in lung adenocarcinoma and NFE2L2 mutations in lung squamous cell carcinoma. Additional associations involving specific EGFR and KRAS mutation subtypes and rarer alterations were observed, but were based on small numbers of cases and should be considered exploratory. Several of the associated genes are involved in the RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, or NRF2-related pathways. However, pathway activation and causality could not be established in this observational study. These findings support further investigation of clinical, histopathological, and molecular factors associated with metastatic progression after surgical resection. Validation in larger, independent, stage-stratified and contemporary cohorts with comprehensive treatment data is required before the identified molecular alterations can be considered for clinical risk stratification or surveillance.

title: Third-generation EGFR-TKI plus pemetrexed-platinum chemotherapy versus TKI monotherapy as first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with brain parenchymal metastases.
authors: Zhou J, Wang Y, Wen K et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of first-line third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) combined with pemetrexed-platinum chemotherapy in patients with EGFR-mutant advanced lung adenocarcinoma and brain parenchymal metastases.
METHODS: A bicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted. A total of 150 eligible patients were enrolled and balanced by 1:1 propensity score matching. Tumor response, survival outcomes, and treatment-related adverse events were compared between groups.
RESULTS: After matching, 60 patients were assigned to each group. The intracranial objective response rate was 78.3% in the combination group versus 61.7% in the monotherapy group (P = 0.046). The median intracranial progression-free survival was 28.3 months in the combination group (hazard ratio = 0.536, 95% confidence interval: 0.350-0.820, P = 0.002). Systemic progression-free survival and overall survival were also significantly prolonged in the combination arm. Adverse events were predominantly chemotherapy-related toxicities and were generally manageable.
CONCLUSION: First-line third-generation EGFR-TKI plus pemetrexed-platinum chemotherapy is associated with superior intracranial and systemic survival benefits in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma patients with brain parenchymal metastases, with a favorable safety profile. This study provides real-world evidence to support clinical treatment decision-making.

title: Antibody-drug conjugates after EGFR-TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: Evidence boundaries, post-progression reassessment, and therapeutic sequencing.
authors: Wang L, Feng Y, Jia R et al.
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are emerging therapeutic options for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) after the development of resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). However, the founding EGFR alteration alone does not guide ADC selection. At progression, actionable resistance mechanisms, altered antigen expression, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, spatial heterogeneity, and histological transformation may shift treatment priorities. This narrative review links agent-specific evidence boundaries to an eight-domain assessment of the post-progression disease state and distinguishes ADC eligibility from therapeutic priority. The framework first identifies clinical scenarios requiring immediate local, CNS-directed, or lineage-specific treatment. It then evaluates resistance-directed therapy and other systemic options in the context of prior treatment. Finally, each ADC is assessed according to its evidence base, biomarkers, construct fit, disease distribution, availability, and patient-specific safety. Currently, selected TROP2-directed ADCs have the most mature evidence. HER3-directed therapy remains under investigation, whereas c-Met- and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-directed ADCs may be relevant in biomarker-defined settings. Tissue biopsy, plasma circulating tumor DNA analysis, and selected cerebrospinal fluid testing should be considered when the findings could alter clinical management. Accordingly, ADCs should be positioned relative to competing local and systemic strategies rather than considered a uniform post-osimertinib class. Prospective validation is required to determine whether this framework improves treatment outcomes.

title: A Self-Assembled Affibody-Drug Conjugate Nanoagent for EGFR-Targeted Synergistic Codelivery of Exatecan and an MDM2 Inhibitory Peptide.
authors: Zhao M, Gao W, Xia X et al.
abstract: Regulation of the tumor suppressor p53 is a promising approach for cancer treatment; however, a single regulatory method often shows limited efficacy. Here, we develop an affibody-drug conjugate nanoagent (ADCN) for the targeted codelivery of topoisomerase I inhibitor DX8591 and p53-MDM2 inhibitor PMI to upregulate p53 levels in cancer cells. The tripartite conjugate ZEGFR:1907-PMI-DX8591 self-assembled into nanoparticles with an average diameter of 74.4 nm, resulting in improved pharmacokinetic profiles and enhanced tumor-targeting ability. After efficient EGFR-mediated cellular uptake, the ZEGFR:1907-PMI-DX8591 ADCN released DX8591 and PMI intracellularly, leading to synergistic p53 activation by inducing p53 production and blocking its degradation. In EGFR-positive non-small cell lung tumor models, the ADCN showed excellent tumor accumulation and achieved 81.7% tumor growth inhibition, which was 1.5-fold and 1.2-fold higher than those of the ZEGFR:1907-PMI and ZEGFR:1907-DX8591 monotherapies, respectively. This affibody-based delivery system provides a promising strategy for synergistic cancer therapy.

title: Exploring the Potential Mechanism of Ethyl Acetate Extract from Tumor Vine in Combination with Cisplatin for Treating Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Based on Network Pharmacology and Cellular Experiments.
authors: Jang L, Qing B, Zhong W et al.
abstract: To investigate the mechanism of the ethyl acetate extract of Tumor Vine (PT-EAE) in combination with cisplatin (DDP) for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), using network pharmacology prediction and validation through cellular experiments. The chemical components of PT-EAE were identified using Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Quadrupole-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometry (UPLC-Q-Exactive-Orbitrap-MS). Network pharmacology was employed to predict the potential active components of PT-EAE and their molecular targets affecting NSCLC cell functions. A "PT-EAE-active components-targets-disease" interaction network was constructed. Gene Ontology (GO) functional annotation and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis were performed on the potential targets to identify core targets and signaling pathways closely related to the active components of PT-EAE. Subsequently, in A549 cells, the effects of PT-EAE alone, DDP alone, and their combination (PT-EAE & DDP) were evaluated. Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay, wound healing assay, transwell assay, and flow cytometry were used to detect cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis, respectively. Finally, western blotting and quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) were utilized to detect the expression levels and phosphorylation status of the predicted core molecular proteins following treatment with PT-EAE and DDP. PT-EAE inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion of A549 cells, while promoting apoptosis. Compared to the DDP monotherapy group, the PT-EAE & DDP combination group reduced the IC50 of DDP for inhibiting A549 cell proliferation. Network pharmacology analysis identified 12 active components in PT-EAE, which were mapped to 124 NSCLC-related targets and multiple key signaling pathways. Among these, EGFR, Src, and PI3K were identified as potential core nodes. At the molecular level, PT-EAE downregulated the protein expression levels of EGFR and Src in A549 cells, as well as the phosphorylation levels of downstream molecules in the Src signaling pathway-PI3K, Akt, and mTOR. It also suppressed the mRNA expression of EGFR, Src, PI3K, Akt, and mTOR. The ethyl acetate extract of Tumor Vine, when combined with cisplatin, shows promising anti-tumor activity through multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway actions, with the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway likely representing one of its therapeutic routes.

title: Discovery and Optimization of Isoform Selective ULK1 Degraders to Enhance Antitumor Activity in KRAS-Mutant Cancer.
authors: Chin Chan S, Bayle S, Lamptey M et al.
abstract: Selective targeting of ULK1 represents a promising approach to overcome autophagy-mediated resistance in KRAS-driven cancers. However, achieving selectivity over the closely related ULK2 isoform with ATP-competitive inhibitors remains challenging due to the high sequence homology within their kinase domains. Here, we describe the design, synthesis, and structure-degradation relationship studies of two cereblon-recruiting ULK1 degraders, MR-9034 and MR-9036. Structure-guided optimization led to the discovery of MR-9036 as a potent and selective ULK1 PROTAC that degrades ULK1 without affecting ULK2 or IMiD neo-substrates. Cellular and biophysical studies confirm ternary complex formation and proteasome-dependent degradation. Compared with the clinical ULK1/2 inhibitor DCC-3116, MR-9036 produces sustained autophagy suppression following compound washout. In KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC models, ULK1 degradation enhances the antiproliferative activity of sotorasib. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) studies in mice support in vivo feasibility. These findings establish selective ULK1 degradation as a chemical strategy to interrogate ULK1 biology and enhance therapeutic response in KRAS-driven cancers.

title: Small Molecules Prescribed On- and Off-Label for Thoracic Cancers During Pregnancy: A Combined VigiBase and Systematic Review Analysis.
authors: Noseda R, Salfi G, Bedussi F et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thoracic cancers during pregnancy are rare but increasingly encountered because of delayed childbearing and the rising incidence of cancer in younger individuals. Despite guideline recommendations, exposure to targeted small-molecule therapies occurs across all trimesters, but safety data remain limited.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the safety of targeted small-molecule therapies for thoracic cancers during pregnancy by combining VigiBase data with a systematic review.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We performed a pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis based on the reporting odds ratio (ROR) and a systematic review. Individual case safety reports from VigiBase (January 1, 2006-February 24, 2026) were analysed. A systematic review of PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus through June 25, 2026 included case reports and case series.
RESULTS: The VigiBase analysis included 15,023 reports of anticancer exposure during pregnancy, of which 162 involved small molecules currently used on- and off-label for thoracic cancers, including 75 with approved agents for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Compared with other anticancer agents, including cytotoxic drugs, immune checkpoint inhibitors, other immunotherapies, antibody-drug conjugates, molecularly targeted therapies (including biologics and small molecules other than those of interest), and anticancer agents not further specified, the small molecules of interest were associated with disproportionate reporting of premature labor (ROR: 2.64; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.21-5.75), foetal growth restriction (ROR: 2.10; 95% CI 1.15-3.84), neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (ROR: 3.78; 95% CI 1.50-9.57), and low birth weight (ROR: 2.27; 95% CI 1.18-4.37). Among approved small molecules for NSCLC, signals were observed for premature labor (ROR: 4.17; 95% CI 1.65-10.53), neonatal respiratory complications (ROR: 2.56; 95% CI 1.02-6.42), and low birth weight (ROR: 3.55; 95% CI 1.61-7.83). Of note, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) inhibitor ICSRs were fewer, and 14/18 alectinib reports described pregnancy exposure without pregnancy-related ADRs of interest, precluding alectinib-specific disproportionality analysis. The systematic review included 26 women (27 pregnancies) with oncogene-driven metastatic NSCLC. Live births occurred in 96.3% of pregnancies, with 53.8% preterm deliveries, 33.3% pregnancy complications, and 19.2% neonatal complications. Maternal outcomes were favourable (objective response rate 80.8%). There were no clinically significant pregnancy complications reported in the 10 cases involving alectinib exposure alone.
CONCLUSIONS: Exposure during pregnancy to small molecules currently used on- and off-label for thoracic cancers was associated with disproportionate reporting signals for selected adverse foetal outcomes. The available clinical evidence remains limited, and although no clinically significant pregnancy complications were reported with alectinib exposure, the current data are insufficient to establish its safety. Treatment decisions should therefore be individualised and made within a multidisciplinary expert setting.

title: Emerging antibody-drug conjugates in lung cancer: highlights from the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting.
authors: Wang X, Miao J, Bao Y et al.
abstract: The 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting presented substantial new data on antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) in lung cancer, highlighting the ongoing expansion of ADC-based strategies from later-line treatment toward first-line combination regimens. This focused narrative review summarizes and discusses the efficacy and safety findings of ADCs targeting TROP2, HER2, Nectin-4, PD-L1, c-Met, B7-H3, DLL3, SEZ6, and other emerging targets in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), with particular attention to emerging ADC plus immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations in the first-line setting. Taken together, these findings highlight an expanding ADC landscape in lung cancer. However, many of the emerging strategies remain supported primarily by preliminary conference-reported or early-phase data and therefore require confirmation in mature peer-reviewed studies and adequately powered randomized clinical trials.

title: Antibody-drug conjugates in advanced small-cell lung cancer: a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis of later-line monotherapy.
authors: Chen X, Li S, Li H
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are being investigated in advanced small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), but the evidence is dominated by early-phase studies conducted in non-exchangeable treatment settings. We evaluated the activity and toxicity of ADCs while separating later-line monotherapy from frontline combination therapy, later-line combination therapy, and post-induction maintenance.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception and in 28 August 2026. ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) were searched on 28 August 2026. We constructed an arm-level dataset that recorded regimen, dose, clinical context, target, outcome definition, numerator, denominator, analysis set, and source. The primary quantitative synthesis was restricted to second-line or later ADC monotherapy; other clinical contexts were summarized descriptively. Single-arm proportions were synthesized using a binomial-normal random-intercept generalized linear mixed model on the logit scale. We reported 95% confidence intervals (CIs), between-study variance, heterogeneity, and 95% prediction intervals. An inverse-variance logit random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp inference was used as a sensitivity analysis. Fixed-time Kaplan-Meier survival estimates and inconsistently defined common adverse events were not pooled.
RESULTS: 16 trial families evaluating eight ADCs across five target classes met the eligibility criteria. In the primary later-line monotherapy analysis, the pooled ORR was 25.7% (95% CI, 16.4%-37.9%), and the pooled DCR was 72.7% (95% CI, 60.7%-82.2%). The pooled incidences of grade ≥3 TEAEs and grade ≥3 TRAEs were 62.8% (95% CI, 59.6%-65.9%) and 45.5% (95% CI, 35.5%-56.0%), respectively. The prediction intervals for ORR, DCR, and grade ≥3 TRAEs were wide. Proportions observed in a new study may therefore differ substantially from the pooled estimates. Frontline combinations, later-line combinations, and maintenance therapy yielded context-specific signals but were not compared with later-line monotherapy. Target-stratified analyses were exploratory; B7-H3 and DLL3 estimates were based on small, non-comparative groups, whereas Trop-2 and SEZ6 were not pooled because fewer than three studies were available.
CONCLUSIONS: Later-line ADC monotherapy showed antitumor activity but frequent clinically important toxicity, with substantial between-study variation. The evidence does not establish superiority by treatment line, regimen, agent, or molecular target; single-arm response estimates also do not demonstrate a survival benefit. Randomized, context-specific trials using harmonized efficacy and safety definitions are needed.

title: Lung Cancer Organoid Models for Studying Resistance to Anti-Angiogenic Therapy: Mechanisms and Applications.
authors: Lin H, Wang K, Chen H et al.
abstract: Anti-angiogenic therapies provide clinically meaningful benefit in selected treatment settings for advanced non-small cell lung cancer, but durable responses are limited by heterogeneous and adaptive resistance. This resistance is not solely tumor-intrinsic; it emerges from interactions among tumor plasticity, compensatory angiogenic signaling, hypoxia, stromal and immune remodeling, vascular recovery, and alternative blood-supply mechanisms. These processes require different biological variables and therefore cannot be adequately interrogated by a single experimental model. Patient-derived lung cancer organoids preserve patient-specific tumor features and are useful for studying tumor-intrinsic responses, but tumor-only organoids do not reproduce perfusion-dependent vascular physiology, permeability, or drug-delivery dynamics. Microenvironment-integrated co-culture, vascularization, and microfluidic or perfusion engineering can extend these capabilities, although model complexity alone does not establish stronger evidence. This review integrates the clinical and mechanistic basis of anti-angiogenic resistance with the capabilities and limitations of current lung cancer organoid models and other three-dimensional systems. We propose a mechanism-matched framework linking the resistance mechanism to the required variable, the minimum set of model capabilities, and claim-matched readouts. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing structural from functional vascularization, tumor drug response from anti-angiogenic resistance, and acute treatment effects from acquired resistance. Current lung cancer organoid systems can model tumor-intrinsic and selected microenvironment-mediated responses and, increasingly, vascular responses, but direct longitudinal evidence of acquired anti-angiogenic resistance remains limited. Future progress will depend on fit-for-purpose standardization, functional qualification, longitudinal modeling, and prospective alignment with clinically observed resistance trajectories.

title: Preclinical Evaluation of B7-H3-Targeted ADC-Based Molecular Imaging in Lung and Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
authors: Sui J, Qin J, Hsu JC et al.
abstract: B7-H3 is widely expressed in multiple solid tumors but shows minimal expression in normal tissues, making it an ideal target for molecular imaging; however, its systematic investigation remains limited. In this study, we utilized the clinically investigated B7-H3-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) HS-20093 to develop and evaluate a novel immuno-positron emission tomography (immuno-PET) tracer, [89Zr]Zr-DFO-HS-20093, for accurate imaging of B7-H3 expression in lung cancer and triple-negative breast cancer models. [89Zr]Zr-DFO-HS-20093 was synthesized with high radiochemical purity (98.2 ± 0.6%). Cellular uptake assays revealed significantly higher tracer uptake in A549 cells than in 4T1 cells at 1, 2, and 4 h (all P < 0.0001), which was markedly reduced by blocking with excess unlabeled antibody. Immunofluorescence revealed predominant membrane localization of B7-H3 in 4T1 cells, whereas A549 cells exhibited pronounced intracellular distribution, suggesting enhanced internalization. In tumor-bearing mice, [89Zr]Zr-DFO-HS-20093 positron emission tomography (PET)/CT enabled clear tumor visualization, with peak uptake at 24 h post-injection in both A549 and 4T1 xenografts (9.63 ± 1.97 and 7.15 ± 3.14 μCi/mL, respectively), supporting its potential for tumor imaging. Ex vivo biodistribution data corroborated the PET findings, showing significantly higher tracer uptake in A549 tumors (5.01 ± 1.19 % ID/g) than in blocked tumors (2.89 ± 0.43 % ID/g) and 4T1 tumors (1.89 ± 0.47 % ID/g) (P = 0.034 and P = 0.003, respectively). Immunohistochemical analysis of A549 xenografts showed strong B7-H3 expression (3+), whereas 4T1 tumors exhibited lower expression levels (1-2+), further confirming that B7-H3 expression patterns were consistent with the imaging results. [89Zr]Zr-DFO-HS-20093 enables sensitive immuno-PET imaging of B7-H3 and reveals tumor-type-dependent differences in B7-H3 expression and intracellular behavior.
