title: Effect of Acupuncture for Loss of Appetite in Advanced Lung Cancer Undergoing Immunotherapy: Protocol of a Randomized Controlled Trial.
authors: Fan J, Zhan Y, Chen H et al.
abstract: BackgroundLoss of appetite (LOA) is a highly prevalent and distressing symptom in advanced lung cancer, leading to malnutrition, poorer treatment tolerance, and reduced quality of life. Although acupuncture may help manage cancer-related symptoms, its effect on LOA in patients receiving immunotherapy is unclear. This study aims to assess the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for alleviating LOA in this population.MethodsThis multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial will enroll 80 eligible patients with advanced lung cancer undergoing immunotherapy who experience LOA, defined as a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) score ≥30 mm. Participants will be randomly assigned to either true acupuncture or sham acupuncture in a 1:1 ratio, administered over 24 sessions within a 12-week period. The primary outcome is the LOA response rate at week 12. Secondary outcomes include changes in LOA severity, nutritional and hematologic markers, patient-reported measures (appetite/cachexia, disease symptoms, psychological distress, and sleep), and tumor response. Safety and blinding success will also be assessed. Data will be analyzed using SPSS 20.0 and R software.DiscussionTo our knowledge, this is the first rigorously designed trial evaluating acupuncture for LOA in advanced lung cancer patients undergoing immunotherapy. The findings may inform integrative supportive care strategies for this patient population.

title: A systematic review and probabilistic meta-analysis of health risks and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) associated with heavy metals in global drinking water: a continental comparison.
authors: Shorif MJU, Chowdhury S, Al-Mamun A et al.
abstract: Heavy metal contamination in drinking water is a public health issue. This study conducted a probabilistic meta-analysis of health risk assessment for six commonly reported heavy metals (arsenic [As], lead [Pb], mercury [Hg], cadmium [Cd], chromium [Cr] and nickel [Ni]) in drinking water across six continents (Asia, Europe, Africa, North America, South America and Oceania) using the data from 2000 to 2024. Human exposure and risks were quantified in terms of cancer risks (CRs) and loss of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Monte Carlo simulation was employed to generate 5,000 random scenarios to incorporate uncertainty in risk assessment. Africa exhibited the average concentrations of As, Pb, Hg, Cd, Cr and Ni in drinking water of 176.7, 123.3, 93.7, 80.2, 91.0 and 35.1 μg/L respectively. The overall averages of CRs in Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Africa and Oceania were predicted to be 3.25 × 10-4, 1.34 × 10-4, 2.26 × 10-4, 1.18 × 10-3, 4.1 × 10-3 and 5.83 × 10-5 respectively while the DALYs were 1.48 × 105, 7.14 × 103, 1.20 × 104, 5.51 × 104, 8.63 × 105 and 2.68 × 102 respectively. Across six continents, inorganic fraction of arsenic (iAs) was the dominant carcinogen, contributing (45-91) % to total cancer risks in Asia, contributions of iAs and Cd were almost similar. The loss of DALYs were highest in Africa (8.63 × 105), due mainly to arsenic-induced bladder and cadmium-induced lung cancers. The global economic burden was USD 29 billion, with Africa accounting for almost 52 %. Sensitivity analysis identified iAs as the key parameter. The heavy metal contamination is a public health issue that requires decisive actions in Africa, South America and Asia.

title: Real-World Comparative Survival Outcomes of First-Line Serplulimab Plus Chemotherapy in Extensive-Stage Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Jing Y, Li M, Li S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) remains an aggressive malignancy with poor survival despite platinum-etoposide chemotherapy. Although serplulimab plus chemotherapy has demonstrated a survival benefit in randomized trials, comparative real-world evidence remains limited. We therefore evaluated survival outcomes with first-line serplulimab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in patients with ES-SCLC.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study at Tianjin Chest Hospital. Patients with ES-SCLC who initiated first-line platinum-etoposide-based chemotherapy between January 2020 and December 2024 were screened, with follow-up censored on May 1, 2025. Patients were classified according to whether serplulimab was incorporated into first-line treatment. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS), and the secondary endpoint was real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Treatment effects were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analyses and Cox proportional hazards models. Because of the limited sample size and event count, the primary adjusted Cox model was restricted to prespecified clinical covariates. Sensitivity analyses included treatment-year adjustment, restriction to patients treated during 2022-2024, reduced propensity score overlap weighting and stabilized trimmed inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW).
RESULTS: The final cohort included 112 patients, of whom 30 received serplulimab plus chemotherapy and 82 received chemotherapy alone. Median OS was 18.69 months with serplulimab plus chemotherapy and 11.86 months with chemotherapy alone (HR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.27-0.90; P = 0.021; log-rank P = 0.017). The association remained significant after parsimonious clinical adjustment (adjusted HR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.27-0.93; P = 0.028). Sensitivity analyses yielded directionally similar OS estimates across treatment-year adjustment, 2022-2024 restriction, overlap weighting, and stabilized trimmed IPTW. Median rwPFS was also numerically longer with serplulimab plus chemotherapy, although the difference was not statistically significant (10.64 vs 8.18 months; HR = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.48-1.20; P = 0.244).
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center real-world cohort, first-line serplulimab plus chemotherapy was associated with longer OS than chemotherapy alone in patients with ES-SCLC, whereas the rwPFS difference was not statistically significant. The findings were directionally supported by multiple sensitivity analyses but should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited sample size, potential calendar-time confounding, and incomplete standardized safety assessment. Larger prospective studies are needed for confirmation.

title: Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy.
authors: Vino D SK, Gebski V, Senthi S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radiation therapy (RT) is indicated for 77% of patients with lung cancer. Over 20% of patients are affected by radiation-induced lung injury. Computed tomography ventilation imaging (CTVI) estimates high and low functioning lung regions. During RT planning, CTVI can guide preferential avoidance of higher ventilated regions by redirecting dose to less well ventilated regions, sparing healthy lung tissue. The double-masked randomized Trans-Tasman Radiation Oncology Group (TROG) 21.08 VITaL trial will investigate if sparing healthy lung can improve the quality of life (QoL) for patients with stage 3 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT.
METHODS: 165 patients will be recruited to test the hypothesis that patients receiving healthy lung-sparing RT have better QoL than patients receiving standard RT. CTVI will be generated from exhale and inhale breath-hold CT scan pairs. A healthy lung-sparing plan and a standard treatment plan will be created for each patient and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio for the patient's treatment. QoL will be assessed with the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Lung questionnaire before and after treatment. Secondary hypotheses include that patients in the healthy lung-sparing arm will have fewer treatment side effects, better lung function, be more likely to receive and complete adjuvant immunotherapy, and healthy lung-sparing treatment will be cost-effective. Patient follow-up will continue for three years.
DISCUSSION: This prospective randomized trial will determine whether the incorporation of healthy lung-sparing RT based on CTVI improves QoL, reduces pulmonary toxicity, and increases eligibility to receive curative immunotherapy for patients with stage 3 NSCLC.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06127654).

title: InDuRanS: neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy followed by surgery or definitive chemoradiotherapy and consolidation durvalumab in resectable and borderline resectable stage IIB-IIIA/B non-small-cell lung cancer.
authors: Gkika E, Waller CF, Dejonckheere CS et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal integration of surgery and definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) following modern neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in stage IIB-IIIA/B non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains controversial. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors have substantially improved outcomes in both resectable and unresectable disease, prospective randomized data directly comparing surgery and definitive CRT after neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy are lacking.
METHODS: InDuRanS is a prospective, multicenter, randomized, open-label phase II trial conducted in Germany. Patients with (borderline) resectable stage IIB-IIIA/B (N2) NSCLC receive three cycles of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy with durvalumab plus platinum-paclitaxel. Patients with persistent resectability are randomized 1:1 to surgery or definitive CRT. Both treatment arms receive consolidation durvalumab for up to 12 months. The primary endpoint is 2-year event-free survival in 158 randomized patients. Key secondary endpoints include progression-free survival, overall survival, safety and tolerability, health-related quality of life, and an extensive exploratory translational research program.
DISCUSSION: InDuRanS is the first randomized trial to directly compare surgery versus definitive CRT within a contemporary multimodal treatment sequence incorporating both neoadjuvant and consolidation immunotherapy in stage IIB-IIIA/B NSCLC. Its results are expected to help define optimal local treatment strategies in an evolving therapeutic landscape. InDuRanS is currently active and open to enrollment as of April 2025, with primary completion anticipated in 2028 (NCT06810609).

title: LLM-assisted multidisciplinary decision-making in lung cancer: efficacy of Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5 in a real-world MDT setting.
authors: Zhou Z, Wang M, Li J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multidisciplinary team (MDT) review is essential for individualized treatment planning in lung cancer, where decisions often require integration of staging, pathology, molecular findings, performance status, and multimodal treatment options. However, the effective implementation of MDT review remains constrained by limited specialist availability in resource-limited hospitals and by high patient volume, heavy physician workload, and tight clinical schedules in tertiary care centers. Large language models (LLMs) may support MDT workflows by synthesizing clinical information and generating preliminary treatment recommendations for clinician review. This study compared GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro with expert MDT recommendations in real-world lung cancer cases and evaluated how information completeness and input format influenced LLM-generated treatment recommendations.
METHODS: We conducted a head-to-head evaluation of GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro for lung-cancer multidisciplinary team decision support. For each of 150 consecutively collected cases, structured vignettes were entered using three information-completeness levels in both natural-language and isomorphic JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) formats. Each model produced a single-sentence recommendation. Outputs were compared with the expert multidisciplinary team plan, which was treated as a clinical reference standard for concordance analysis rather than an objective guideline-only gold standard, using predefined plan-level categories. To better quantify model performance, we applied keyword extraction and semantic matching to normalize both multidisciplinary team recommendations and model outputs into ten treatment categories with subsequent manual review and correction.
RESULTS: Stratifying by information level and format, Information Level III produced the best overall performance for Gemini-2.5-Pro under natural-language input, with F1 0.7603, accuracy 0.8647, precision 0.7031, and recall 0.8278. GPT-5 achieved its highest recall under Information Level III with JSON input (recall 0.9132), but this was accompanied by lower precision and F1. Under the same natural-language Information Level III, GPT-5 reached recall 0.8770 with F1 0.6826 and accuracy 0.7967.
CONCLUSIONS: Gemini-2.5-Pro show promise as adjuncts to MDT decision-making in lung cancer, offering high agreement with expert plans under controlled conditions. With appropriate clinician oversight, LLM-based tools may help expand access to standardized, high-quality recommendations where specialist availability is limited.

title: The prognostic value of physical functioning on survival in patients with nonsmall cell lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Arents E, Haesevoets S, Van Overbeke M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physical functioning has emerged as a potentially valuable prognostic indicator in patients with nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of objectively measured components of physical functioning on survival outcomes across treatment modalities.
METHODS: Medline, Web of Science and Scopus were searched up to May 2025. Eligible studies included adult patients with NSCLC and assessed at least one objectively measured physical functioning indicator in relation to survival outcomes. Indicators were categorised using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework into "body functions and structures", "activities" and "participation" and studies were stratified into "surgery" and "nonsurgery" groups. Meta-analyses were conducted when data permitted it.
RESULTS: 58 studies (19 436 patients) were included. Most assessments were performed before treatment. In the surgical group, only "activities"-based measures were evaluated. A meta-analysis restricted to this group showed that survivors had substantially higher (functional) exercise capacity, measured through cardiopulmonary exercise testing and field tests (standardised mean difference 0.79). In nonsurgical cohorts, prognostic value extended across all ICF domains, with low handgrip strength (hazard ratio (HR) 1.27), low (functional) exercise capacity (HR 2.11) and physical inactivity (HR 2.86) associated with significantly higher mortality. Notably, no studies in surgical cohorts evaluated "body functions" or "participation". Heterogeneity and varying thresholds were noted across studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Objectively measured physical functioning is a significant prognostic indicator of survival in NSCLC. Routine assessment could enhance risk stratification and guide personalised care. Future research should address longitudinal changes, standardisation of measures and targeted interventions.

title: Interventions to increase participation in lung cancer screening programmes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Djuric O, Guida A, Bononi F et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We aimed to systematically review and meta-analyse the effectiveness of interventions in increasing informed choice and participation in lung cancer screening based on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT).
METHODS: Five electronic databases, Medline (PubMed version), Embase, Cinahl (Ebsco version), Scopus and Cochrane CENTRAL, were searched for randomised controlled trials, nonrandomised controlled trials and before-after studies published from 2000 until 15 March 2023. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to assess the effectiveness of interventions to increase rates of LDCT completion.
RESULTS: Out of 3483 studies identified, 14 completed and 21 ongoing studies were included in the review. Shared-decision making (SDM)+navigation (OR 4.34, 95% CI 2.50-7.54) and outreach+navigation (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.70-2.84) resulted in a higher proportion of LDCT performed compared to the control group. Educational/informational interventions (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.89-1.19) as well as SDM alone (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.57-2.32) did not improve LDCT uptake, despite the second improving decisional outcomes in both intervention and control groups. Multicomponent interventions showed significantly higher LDCT uptake (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.79-3.90), compared to unicomponent interventions (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.14). The vast majority of interventions, including those in ongoing trials, are patient-oriented, while community-based, provider-level and system-level interventions remain rare.
CONCLUSIONS: Combining high-intensity patient-oriented interventions, such as patient navigation, active outreach and SDM, appears to be the most promising strategy to increase lung cancer screening uptake (low certainty of evidence). However, implementation studies are needed to evaluate interventions targeting both provider and healthcare systems level.

title: How to plan and deliver lung cancer reirradiation: A consensus approach from the ESTRO reirradiation and lung focus groups and ReCOG.
authors: Hoffmann L, Matrosic CK, Andratschke N et al.
abstract: Lung reirradiation is seeing increased use, yet the evidence base guiding its practice remains limited despite significant technological advances. This paper provides a consensus approach addressing the technical factors underpinning clinical decision-making. It aims to answer the central question: how can clinical teams implement a safe, reproducible, and technically robust workflow for high-dose lung reirradiation? The recommendations are developed by an expert panel of radiation oncologists, medical physicists, and radiation therapists (RTT) from 14 European, American, and Canadian centres, synthesizing a broad range of clinical perspectives. The scope of this work/manuscript is to provide a structured, practical workflow applicable across diverse clinical settings. Using a clinical case, the manuscript demonstrates key conceptual principles, such as the rationale for advanced dose accumulation and the impact of anatomical changes during treatment, with clear, stepwise guidance to support consistent implementation and informed clinical judgement. Key recommended steps include retrieval of prior treatment data; consideration of prior positioning and motion management; and equieffective dose accumulation using deformable image registration or organ-at-risk (OAR)-focused rigid registration. Treatment planning should explicitly incorporate prior dose while balancing target coverage against OAR limits. Daily online volumetric image guidance is central to evaluating both bony and soft-tissue anatomy, enabling setup adjustments to protect critical structures approaching tolerance. Clear documentation and multidisciplinary communication are integral throughout. This consensus approach is intended to support both centres that aim to establish reirradiation practice and experienced teams seeking to harmonize best practices.

title: Serial circulating tumour DNA monitoring in first-line advanced NSCLC (COPE): a randomized, two-arm non-comparative phase II trial.
authors: Tambaoan CFB, Phan L, Cousin S et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: COPE evaluated serial circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling with molecular tumor board (MTB) review during first-line therapy for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: COPE was a multicenter, randomized (2:1), noncomparative phase II trial. Arm A underwent serial plasma profiling with every report reviewed at a weekly virtual MTB; Arm B received standard management. The primary endpoint was 18-month overall survival (OS) in Arm A versus a prespecified 40% historical benchmark; no between-arm comparison was planned.
RESULTS: Among 176 patients, 117 were assigned to Arm A and 59 to Arm B. Eighteen-month OS was 53.8% (95% CI, 44.3-62.5) and 65.7% (95% CI, 52.0-76.3), respectively. Baseline plasma profiling provided contributory information in 32 of 35 patients with noncontributory or unavailable tissue, increasing genotyping success from 69% to 97%. Paired baseline and early on-treatment samples were available in 90 patients (median, 21 days; range, 19-64). ctDNA clearance was associated with higher objective response rate (83% vs. 52%), longer progression-free survival (22.9 vs. 5.4 months; P<0.001), and longer OS (not reached vs. 17.1 months; P=0.004) than persistent detection.
CONCLUSIONS: Serial ctDNA profiling with weekly MTB review was operationally feasible and complemented tissue genotyping. Clinical benefit was not demonstrated; early ctDNA kinetics require validation in interventional trials.

title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer.
authors: Englander RP, Brugiolo M, Devoucoux M et al.
abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

title: Global, regional and national cancer burden and trends of middle-aged and older populations: a GBD 2021-based analysis, prediction and prevention.
authors: Sun R, Shi F, Tang Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Middle-aged and older adults (MAOs; defined as individuals aged ≥40 years) account for the global cancer burden, contributing to 70-80% of cases. Characterizing cancer profiles in this demographic is essential for developing targeted prevention and treatment strategies to mitigate global impacts.
METHODS: Using Global Burden of Diseases (GBD) 2021 data, we analyzed incidence, prevalence, mortality and Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) for 31 cancers among MAOs (aged≥40) across 204 countries/21 regions(1990-2021). Trends were quantified via Joinpoint regression, and autoregressive integrated moving-average (ARIMA) models projected the burden through 2035. Risk attribution utilized population attributable fractions across Socio-demographic Index (SDI) quintiles. An order-independent Shapley decomposition attributed projected cancer incidence changes during 2021-2035 to population growth, aging, and age-specific incidence rate shifts.
RESULTS: In 2021, MAOs accounted for 48,804,114 incident cases and 9,434,210 deaths. Females exhibited a 1.14-fold higher age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) than males, yet males had a higher age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR). Projections suggested a continued rise in cancer burden through 2035. Peak incidence occurred in ages 60-69 and the highest mortality in ages 70-79. Breast cancer was the main cancer in females; tracheal/bronchus/lung cancer in males. Tracheal/bronchus/lung cancer dominated mortality across all groups except middle-aged women (breast cancer). High-SDI regions bore the greatest burden, characterized by tracheal/bronchus/lung and colorectal cancers, while low-SDI regions shifted toward breast, cervical and stomach cancer. Risk factor analysis from 2010-2021 revealed rising metabolic risks, with high body mass index (BMI) and fasting plasma glucose-attributable DALYs increasing by 12.39% and 11.36% respectively, especially in high-SDI regions. Conversely, while most behavioral risks declined, smoking remained the leading risk factor, contributing over 60% to lung cancer DALYs. In low-SDI regions, behavioral drivers such as unsafe sex (accounting for >90% of cervical cancer risk) and air pollution remained the dominant persistent risks.
DISCUSSION: This study, the first focusing on MAOs' global cancer burden, reveals heterogeneous patterns by age, gender, and SDI. Lung cancer was the leading cause of death (smoking as main risk). Metabolic risks rose in high-SDI regions, behavioral risks in low-SDI regions. In conclusion, MAOs' cancer burden will rise through 2035; region-specific precision strategies are essential.

title: Insights into extracellular vesicles: From biogenesis and tumor immune modulation to their clinical potential in immunotherapy.
authors: Ma S, Qi A, Wu J et al.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) constitute a key mode of intercellular communication that remodels the complex tumor immune microenvironment by delivering diverse bioactive cargoes between tumor and immune cells. Nucleic acid species, encompassing microRNAs (miRNAs), messenger RNA (mRNAs), and other RNA transcripts, are functionally potent EV cargoes whose selective packaging dictates downstream immune signaling output. This review describes the molecular mechanisms driving selective RNA sorting into EVs, emphasizing sequence-motif recognition and core RNA-binding proteins FMR1 and TRIM25, which govern the enrichment of distinct RNA populations. We illustrate how EV-shuttled RNA molecules elicit context-dependent functional changes across regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and macrophages to shape antitumor or pro-tumor immune states. It critically integrates liquid biopsy evidence for EV-borne RNAs and EV-associated programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) as predictive biomarkers of immunotherapy response in melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma and dissects technical confounders such as non-vesicular RNA contamination and inconsistent isolation protocols. This review further compares nucleic acid loading strategies for native EVs versus cell-membrane-mimetic nanovesicles and explores their applicability for mRNA-based nanovaccines and combinatorial immunotherapy. We highlight underappreciated translational obstacles, noting that harmonized analytical standards, strict encapsulated cargo validation, and independent prospective multicenter trials are essential to translate EV-nucleic acid signatures into personalized cancer immunotherapy.

title: Sarcoid-like Reaction With Pleural Involvement After Neoadjuvant Chemo-immunotherapy For Lung Cancer: A Rare Mimic of Disease Progression.
authors: Coussement A, Van Mol P, Boeckxstaens L et al.
abstract: We report a patient with stage IIA (cT2bN0M0) lung adenocarcinoma who developed new diffuse pleural, pulmonary, and nodal FDG uptake on 18FDG-PET/CT after three cycles of neoadjuvant nivolumab plus cisplatin-pemetrexed, with slight regression of the primary tumour. These findings raised the diagnostic dilemma between disease progression and immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-related sarcoid-like reaction (SLR). Rapid clinical and metabolic improvement after corticosteroid therapy supported SLR, which was subsequently confirmed histologically by noncaseating granulomas without viable tumour at surgery. This case highlights pleural involvement in SLR as a rare and diagnostically challenging immune-related adverse event.

title: Case Report: Fatal varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with Froin-like cerebrospinal fluid and hydrocephalus following pembrolizumab-containing chemoimmunotherapy.
authors: Shen F, Fan S, Wang Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), central nervous system (CNS) infections may mimic or coexist with neurological immune-related adverse events (irAEs). ICI-driven immune dysregulation has been proposed to amplify inflammation against latent pathogens ("immunotherapy infections due to dysregulated immunity", ITI-DI), but this remains a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated diagnosis.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 54-year-old man with stage IIIC lung adenocarcinoma developed a herpes zoster eruption and lumbosacral pain 7 days after the first infusion of pembrolizumab-containing chemoimmunotherapy, followed by rapidly progressive flaccid paraplegia, urinary incontinence, and declining consciousness. Intravenous acyclovir was not initiated until 20 days after rash onset. The first cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample was xanthochromic and coagulated spontaneously in the collection tube (Froin-like CSF), precluding protein measurement. A second lumbar puncture showed mild pleocytosis (8 cells/ μ L; 70% neutrophils) and undetectable glucose; varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected in CSF by post-mortem targeted polymerase chain reaction. Spinal Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse meningeal enhancement; follow-up cranial imaging showed acute hydrocephalus. Despite intravenous acyclovir, corticosteroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin, the patient died 43 days after pembrolizumab initiation.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights VZV CNS infection as an important diagnostic consideration in ICI-treated patients who develop herpes zoster and neurological symptoms, because infection may mimic or coexist with a neurological irAE. The temporal relationship with pembrolizumab raises, but does not establish, the possibility that PD-1 blockade modified the inflammatory response. Prompt virological testing and adequately dosed antiviral therapy are central to management; the role of adjunctive immunomodulation remains uncertain and should be individualized.

title: T Cell Receptor-Engineered T Cell Therapy in Solid Tumors: Where We Stand and What's to Come.
authors: Ferriol-Martínez C, D'Angelo SP
abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.

title: Outcomes of CD20-targeting CAR T-cell therapy in patients with advanced melanoma: MB-CART20.1 Melanoma phase I trial.
authors: Balke-Want H, Theurich S, Gödel P et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies identified CD20+ cells within the melanoma tumor microenvironment, including tumor-associated B-cells and putative cancer stem cells (CSC), as potential therapeutic targets. We therefore evaluated CD20-targeting CAR T-cells in patients with advanced melanoma.
METHODS: This prospective, open-label phase I trial evaluated a 3 +3 design in patients with advanced melanoma, refractory to approved treatments, to assess safety and preliminary activity of autologous anti-CD20 CAR T-cells (MB-CART20.1). Following lymphodepleting chemotherapy, patients received a single MB-CART20.1 infusion. Primary endpoints were safety and tolerability; secondary endpoints included kinetics and early evidence for antitumor activity. Three patients received dose level 1 (DL1) (1.0 ×10⁵ cells/kg) and four patients DL2 (1.0 ×10⁶ cells/kg).
RESULTS: No DLTs occurred at DL1, while two patients experienced DLTs at DL2 (grade 3 ICANS and grade 4 hepatotoxicity). Overall, 43 serious TEAEs were reported across all seven patients. Stable disease was observed in three patients at week 16; all had progressed by month 6. All had received immune checkpoint inhibitors within 6 months before leukapheresis and showed reduced exhaustion marker expression on CD8+ T-cells. In addition, the frequency of CD19+CD24+CD27+ Breg cells trended to associate with progressive disease and inversely correlate with toxicity. MB-CART20.1 showed robust in vivo expansion however, severe DLTs at DL2 without durable clinical benefit led to early trial termination.
CONCLUSIONS: In advanced melanoma, MB-CART20.1 was associated with marked expansion and toxicity, suggesting that Breg depletion and the melanoma-typical treatment history might have driven distinct CAR T-associated immunotoxicities.

title: EGFRvIII-Positive Glioblastoma: Structural Rewiring, Immune Microenvironmental Remodeling, and Therapeutic Resistance.
authors: Ye H, Qiu J, Zhu F et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) harboring EGFRvIII represents a biologically distinct and highly aggressive tumor subset characterized by aberrant receptor signaling, marked intratumoral heterogeneity, and profound immune remodeling. Rather than acting as a constitutively active truncated receptor, EGFRvIII represents a structurally rewired EGFR variant whose altered extracellular architecture, receptor assembly, and trafficking promote ligand-independent signaling and signaling plasticity, thereby supporting tumor proliferation, stemness, invasion, and angiogenesis. Beyond tumor-intrinsic effects, EGFRvIII also contributes to the formation of a spatially heterogeneous, myeloid-dominant and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by myeloid-cell expansion, impaired T cell effector function, and mesenchymal-like tumor-immune plasticity. Despite extensive therapeutic efforts including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, immune checkpoint blockade, and EGFRvIII-targeted CAR-T cell strategies, durable clinical efficacy remains limited by the interplay of antigen heterogeneity, adaptive signaling, clonal evolution, and microenvironmental immunosuppression. Taken together, EGFRvIII can be viewed as a structural and evolutionary regulator that links receptor rewiring and signaling plasticity with immune ecosystem remodeling and therapeutic resistance, underscoring the need for integrated strategies that target both tumor cell-intrinsic signaling and the suppressive microenvironment.

title: Chemokines as regulators of CAR-T cell trafficking, function, and context-dependent tumor cell death.
authors: Levchuk K, Petukhov A, Tursymbek S et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, yet its efficacy in solid tumors remains limited by inefficient trafficking, suppressive myeloid and regulatory T-cell populations, and metabolic stress. These barriers contribute to incomplete tumor cell killing and loss of CAR-T cell function. Chemokines are usually viewed as migratory guides, but in solid tumors they also orchestrate immune cell positioning and inflammatory state. In this review, we discuss how chemokine gradients form inflammatory niches and control CAR-T-cell recruitment, intratumoral distribution, retention, and egress. We also examine how chemokine programs interact with cytokine signaling and regulated tumor cell death to shape local and potentially tissue-wide antitumor immunity, including through the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Finally, we outline translational strategies that include engineered chemokines and matched chemokine receptor programs to enhance the efficacy of chemokine/cytokine-armored CAR-T cells, and related combination therapies.

title: The role of personalised medicine in treating high-risk neuroblastoma in paediatric patients.
authors: Ammeti D, Curci D, Franzin M et al.
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is one of the most challenging paediatric malignancies, accounting for 15% of childhood cancer-related deaths. It is characterised by a high heterogeneity ranging from spontaneous regression to high frequency of metastatic disease at diagnosis. Although current treatment strategies, including chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy, have improved outcomes, recurrence often occurs in high-risk NB patients, thus affecting overall survival. In this context, personalised medicine is emerging as a promising approach taking advantage of predictive biomarkers to refine risk stratification and to predict treatment response, together with the development of innovative treatments for high-risk NB. This review summarises the landscape of biomarkers in NB, focusing on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic signatures associated with aggressive disease biology, therapeutic resistance, and clinical outcome. We highlight how improved patient stratification could help to identify actionable targets resulting in innovative therapeutic strategies. These include GD2-directed immunotherapy, CAR-T and CAR-NK cell approaches, and pathway-directed agents targeting mainly ALK, and MYCN-associated dependencies. Ultimately, the transition from standardised protocols to a systematic integration of multidimensional biomarker profiles with next-generation therapies promises to transform the clinical management of high-risk NB. Addressing the biological complexity of NB ensures more effective and less toxic interventions, paving the way for personalised therapeutic approaches aimed at preventing relapse in high-risk cases and significantly improving long-term survival.

title: Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages in breast cancer: from myeloid plasticity and tumor-promoting programs to CAR-macrophage therapy.
authors: Heydari F, Derakhshani M, Naghinezhad J
abstract: Breast cancer develops within spatially organized, multicellular microenvironments in which particular tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) states can influence immune access and stromal remodeling. Conventional M1/M2 classification and total macrophage density fail to capture the developmental, transcriptional, metabolic, and spatial heterogeneity that determines TAM function. This macrophage-focused review examines breast cancer within its multicellular microenvironment, integrating lineage-tracing, single-cell, spatial, mechanistic, and clinical evidence while distinguishing breast-specific findings from hypotheses extrapolated from other tumors. We examine how tissue-resident and monocyte-derived macrophages are recruited, retained, expanded, and reprogrammed across primary and metastatic sites, emphasizing interactions with malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, vasculature, adipose tissue, and lymphoid populations. In defined breast-tumor contexts, TAM programs have been implicated in immune exclusion, invasion, metastatic dissemination, and adaptation to systemic treatment, although evidence strength varies across mechanisms and therapeutic modalities. Small and heterogeneous clinical studies have not established a benefit from broad CSF1/CSF1R-axis targeting in breast cancer, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Accordingly, we highlight a shift toward state-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated targeting. Emerging approaches include restoring phagocytosis, disrupting chemokine and fibrotic circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and converting suppressive TAMs into inflammatory, antigen-presenting effectors. A major focus is chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy, which combines antigen-directed phagocytosis with tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and recruitment of endogenous immunity. Although early clinical data support manufacturing feasibility, tumor trafficking, and acceptable initial safety, limited antitumor activity underscores challenges involving antigen heterogeneity, persistence, metabolic fitness, biodistribution, and scalable production. We propose a translational roadmap integrating spatial biomarkers, quantitative target selection, macrophage-adapted CAR design, checkpoint-resistant phagocytosis, metabolic engineering, safety switches, and biomarker-guided combination therapy. This framework positions macrophage reprogramming as a context-dependent strategy for modifying selected breast-tumor niches, with therapeutic targets chosen according to the macrophage program and its surrounding cellular architecture.

title: Histone deacetylase inhibition induces an antitumor IRF8-dependent trained immunity-like status in macrophages.
authors: Qin X, Xiang M, Guo Y et al.
abstract: Epigenetic reprogramming underlies innate immune memory. However, whether trained immunity can be induced via epigenetic intervention to combat tumors, and the key regulators controlling this process, remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi) priming establishes a trained immunity-like state in monocytes/macrophages, conferring potent antitumor effect in multiple models of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in female mice. Interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) is identified as the master regulator of the inflammatory transcriptional program, which is governed by IRF8-associated super-enhancers and reinforced by HDACi. Myeloid-specific IRF8 deficiency impairs pro-inflammatory macrophage differentiation and abrogates HDACi-induced antitumor efficacy. Moreover, an IRF8-driven, CCL8-expressing macrophage subset recruits and activates cytotoxic CCR5+CD8+ T cells in the TNBC microenvironment. As a proof-of-principle with translational relevance, CCL8-overexpressing EGFR-targeted CAR T cells exhibit enhanced trafficking and improved efficacy in a humanized TNBC model. Our study defines the IRF8-CCL8-CCR5 axis as an epigenetically potentiated nexus of innate and adaptive antitumor immunity.

title: Cell-based therapies for malignant glioma.
authors: Mooney R, Abd El-Fattah EE, Ngai G et al.
abstract: Despite innovative progress, cellular therapies have not produced durable, population-level survival gains in glioblastoma. Across 3 major modalities, engineered effectors such as chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) and natural killer (NK) cells, immune-education platforms such as dendritic and whole-cell vaccines, and carrier cells delivering oncolytic or drug payloads, trials have shown measurable bioactivity, but durability has varied. This likely reflects systemic barriers, including therapy-induced lymphopenia, myeloid dominance, and T-cell sequestration, as well as local barriers such as antigen heterogeneity and immune suppression. To understand why some studies nevertheless showed more favorable efficacy signals, we reviewed clinical outcomes across these modalities and identified 4 recurring design features that appeared repeatedly among studies reporting more favorable survival signals: treatment in the minimal residual disease setting, a T-helper type 1 supportive context, broadened antigenic coverage, and effective immune hand-off from the initiating therapy to endogenous or adoptively transferred effectors. Across heterogeneous early-phase studies, greater feature alignment sometimes co-occurred with more favorable signals, although this retrospective pattern is descriptive and does not establish association or causality. These observations may help guide future biomarker-informed strategies and provide a practical framework for organizing multimodal trials aimed at converting transient bioactivity into more durable, polyclonal control.

title: Internalizing RGD (iRGD)-modified liposomal nanoparticles as a universal antigen-delivering platform for remodeling tumors and enhancing T-cell receptor-engineered T cell immunotherapy.
authors: Qi H, Zhang H, Wang C et al.
abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T cell (TCR-T) therapy holds promise for solid tumors but faces challenges from insufficient and non-uniform antigen presentation and inefficient T-cell tumor delivery. Current strategies that rely on endogenous tumor antigen expression are often limited by transcriptional silencing or downregulation of target antigens in a substantial fraction of tumor cells, resulting in incomplete tumor recognition. To address this, we developed iRGD-modified liposomal nanoparticles (iRNY-LNPs) as a universal antigen-delivering platform for remodeling tumors and enhancing TCR-T immunotherapy. The iRNY-LNPs, co-assembled from DSPE-PEG-iRGD and DSPE-PEG-NY-ESO-1 (New York Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma-1), exhibited a uniform size of 206.3 ± 5.4 nm and demonstrated significantly enhanced penetration into 3D tumor spheroids compared to non-targeted nanoparticles. In vitro, iRNY-LNPs enabled uniform NY-ESO-1 antigen presentation on tumor cells, potently activating TCR-T cells and enhancing interferon-γ secretion and cytotoxicity. In vivo imaging confirmed efficient tumor accumulation and retention of iRNY-LNPs. In a gastric cancer model, the combination of iRNY-LNPs and NY-ESO-1 TCR-T cells achieved 73.0% tumor growth inhibition and significantly prolonged survival, with no observed systemic toxicity. This study establishes a proactive tumor-remodeling strategy that circumvents the reliance on endogenous antigen expression by enforcing uniform antigen display. Given its modular design based on lipid-peptide conjugates, the platform can be readily adapted to deliver other tumor-associated antigens by simply substituting the peptide moiety, offering a versatile framework for TCR-T immunotherapy against diverse solid tumors.

title: Engineered NKG2C+ CD8+ TKLR cells exhibit effective antitumor control in mice while mitigating cytokine release syndrome.
authors: Lupo KB, Panjwani MK, Halawi AG et al.
abstract: Engineered T and NK cell therapies have widely been used to treat hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, with promising clinical results. Current chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapeutics are, however, associated with treatment-related adverse events such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and are prone to immunologic exhaustion. CAR-NK therapeutics, while not associated with CRS, have limited in vivo persistence. We now demonstrate that a population of NK-like TCRαβ+ CD8 T cells (TKLR), identified and expanded ex vivo through its expression of the activating receptor NKG2C, can be transduced to express a second-generation CD19 CAR (1928z). These CAR+ TKLR demonstrates superior tumor clearance and longer persistence compared to 1928z CAR+ conventional CD8 T cells (TConv) and 1928z CAR+ NK cells in mouse xenograft models. Moreover, CAR-modified TKLR had decreased expression of PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3 and elicited significantly reduced CRS compared to CAR+ CD8 TConv in mouse xenograft models. Similarly, NKG2C+ TKLR engineered with a TCR targeting the NY-ESO-1 antigen exhibited robust tumor control compared to TCR-engineered CD8 TConv in a mouse xenograft model. These data establish NKG2C+ TKLR as a promising platform for cell engineering, and offer a safer, more durable alternative to conventional CAR-T and CAR-NK therapies.

title: Novel approaches to target prostate cancer stem cells driving therapy resistance and cancer progression.
authors: Alatawi FS
abstract: Prostate cancer remains one of the most common malignancies in men, and its global burden continues to rise. Although androgen deprivation therapy and other standard treatments can provide substantial disease control, advanced tumors may progress to castration-resistant prostate cancer, which is associated with poor outcomes. Preclinical and translational evidence implicates prostate cancer stem-like cells (PCSCs) in treatment persistence, progression, and relapse, without establishing them as the sole cause of resistance in patients. PCSC-associated states share functional traits with normal stem cells, including self-renewal and survival under stress; reduced androgen receptor activity occurs in some, but not all, stem-like populations. Their behavior is influenced by the genomic context, including PTEN loss, TP53/RB1 alterations, SPOP mutations, and TMPRSS2-ERG rearrangements, as well as hypoxia, stromal interactions, and inflammatory signaling. These alterations are not specific markers of PCSC identity. Multiple interconnected pathways, notably PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, Hedgehog, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo, JAK/STAT, Notch, EGFR, and hypoxia-driven HIF signaling, provide candidate therapeutic targets. Additional strategies include modifying the microenvironment to suppress epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity, restoring tumor-suppressive microRNAs, and developing checkpoint inhibitors, vaccines, and CAR-T cells against relevant tumor-associated antigens. Most PCSC-specific evidence remains experimental, even when a pathway-directed agent has clinical activity or regulatory approval in a molecularly selected prostate cancer population. Clinical tumor responses do not by themselves demonstrate selective PCSC depletion. This narrative review distinguishes mechanistic findings from clinical outcomes and considers limitations involving marker specificity, model selection, drug delivery, toxicity, and therapeutic escape. Functionally validated biomarkers and appropriately designed combination trials are needed to determine whether targeting PCSC-associated states can improve durable disease control.

title: Site-specific immune remodeling underlies resistance to dual immune checkpoint blockade in metastatic colorectal cancer
summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have limited efficacy in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) with proficient mismatch repair and microsatellite stability (pMMR/MSS), with liver metastases emerging as a dominant determinant of resistance. Whether this reflects a failure to activate antitumor immunity or a failure to direct it remains unclear. We investigated this in the phase II SERPENTINE trial of dual PD-L1 and CTLA-4 blockade by integrating paired pre-treatment and on-treatment single-cell transcriptomic and T-cell receptor (TCR) profiling (388,196 cells; 95,617 clonotypes) metastatic biopsies with deep TCR sequencing of matched peripheral blood (57,902,418 clonotypes). In MSS mCRC, clinical benefit was restricted to patients without liver metastases, whereas all patients with liver metastases progressed. Dual ICI induced systemic T-cell priming regardless of metastatic site, mobilizing therapy-expanded clones that trafficked to both lung and liver lesions, but the fate of this response was determined locally. In lung metastases, therapy-specific clones focused into tissue-resident, proliferative, tumor-reactive CD8+ T-cell states. In liver metastases, the same activation was dispersed: regulatory T cells and suppressive myeloid populations expanded, TCR repertoires diversified, and exhaustion-associated T-cell gene networks fragmented. Cross-lineage co-expression analysis further revealed that tumor proliferation increased in concert with cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell programs, indicating effector engagement that fails to restrain tumor growth. These findings show that resistance to ICI in liver metastases arises from tissue-specific misdirection of immune activation away from productive antitumor immunity, identifying multicellular coordination of the immune response in the metastatic microenvironment as a determinant of therapeutic efficacy.

title: CASTOR1 functional inactivation drives KRAS-mutant NSCLC and therapy resistance by a noncanonical mechanism of tumor suppression.
authors: Wang X, Ding L, Meng W et al.
abstract: CASTOR1, a cytosolic arginine sensor and regulator of mTORC1 signaling, is identified here as a tumor suppressor in KRAS-driven non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In a KRASG12D mouse model, CASTOR1 deletion enhances tumor initiation and progression, accompanied by increased proliferation. Although CASTOR1 is rarely mutated or deleted in human cancers, its expression progressively declines during tumor progression and is associated with increased AKT activation and CASTOR1 phosphorylation, consistent with functional inactivation. Loss of CASTOR1 results in constitutive mTORC1 hyperactivation, impaired arginine-dependent regulation of mTORC1 signaling, elevated p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels, increased AKT and ERK activation, genomic instability, and resistance to KRASG12D inhibitors. Tumors and tumor-derived organoids deficient in CASTOR1 are resistant to KRAS inhibition, but this resistance can be overcome by cotargeting mTORC1 or dual PI3K/mTOR inhibition. These findings identify CASTOR1 as a critical link between nutrient sensing and oncogenic signaling and reveal its functional inactivation as an important mechanism contributing to KRAS-driven NSCLC progression and therapeutic resistance. The results further support rational combination therapies to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance in CASTOR1-low NSCLC.

title: Zidesamtinib: First Approval.
authors: Shirley M
abstract: Zidesamtinib (Jideytro™) is a brain-penetrant, selective small-molecule inhibitor of ROS1 being developed by Nuvalent (a subsidiary of GSK) for the treatment of advanced ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and other solid tumours. ROS1 fusions are oncogenic drivers in a range of cancers and are identified in approximately 1-2% of NSCLCs. Zidesamtinib potently inhibits diverse ROS1 fusion proteins and clinically relevant ROS1 resistance mutations. Further, zidesamtinib has been shown to induce intracranial tumour regression in xenograft models. Supported by findings from the phase I/II ARROS-1 trial, in July 2026, zidesamtinib was approved in the USA for use in the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic ROS1-positive NSCLC who received a prior ROS1 kinase inhibitor. This article summarises the milestones in the development of zidesamtinib leading to this first approval for advanced ROS1-positive NSCLC.

title: Unusual metastatic recurrence of pulmonary adenocarcinoma with a focal neuroendocrine component presenting with bilateral renal metastases and an accompanying pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor-like lesion: a case report.
authors: Ueda T, Miyagawa K, Nakamura K et al.
abstract: A 72-year-old woman with a history of resected lung adenocarcinoma presented with a pancreatic mass and multiple bilateral renal masses. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition of the pancreatic lesion showed neuroendocrine morphology, synaptophysin positivity, focal chromogranin A positivity, and a Ki-67 labeling index of 2%, leading to an initial diagnosis of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor grade 1. Renal biopsy also demonstrated neuroendocrine differentiation with a Ki-67 labeling index of 17%. However, the pancreatic lesion was hypovascular and poorly defined, and the multifocal bilateral renal involvement was atypical for a low-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Re-evaluation of the resected lung specimen revealed a focal neuroendocrine component showing large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma-like features, although the strict diagnostic criteria for such a diagnosis were not fully met. Genomic analysis identified a KRAS G12V mutation shared by the renal and lung tumors, supporting the interpretation that the renal lesions represented metastatic recurrence of the previously resected lung tumor. Direct molecular confirmation was unavailable for the pancreatic lesion because of insufficient residual endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition material; therefore, its origin remained diagnostically uncertain. Nevertheless, based on the overall clinicopathological context, the pancreatic lesion was interpreted as an accompanying neuroendocrine tumor-like lesion most consistent with metastatic recurrence. This case highlights the importance of integrating clinical history, imaging features, disease distribution, archival pathology, and molecular findings when evaluating neuroendocrine tumor-like lesions in patients with a prior malignancy.

title: Comment on: "Impact of ALK rearrangement on survival in resected lung adenocarcinoma: A real-world analysis": Toward risk-adapted adjuvant therapy beyond ALINA.

title: Real-world effectiveness and safety of lurbinectedin in previously treated small cell lung cancer: results from Jazz EMERGE 402.
authors: Badin FB, Lammers PE, Liu G et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), lurbinectedin is approved for first-line maintenance treatment with atezolizumab and as monotherapy following disease progression, but prospective real-world data on its use are lacking.
METHODS: Jazz EMERGE 402 was a prospective, observational, phase 4 trial (NCT04894591) that evaluated lurbinectedin for previously treated SCLC in a diverse, real-world population. The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR). Key secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety.
RESULTS: As of July 17, 2025, 267 patients received ≥ 1 lurbinectedin dose. At baseline, the median age was 67 years, 52 (19%) patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score ≥ 2, 67 (25%) had brain metastases, and 88 (33%) had platinum-resistant disease. ORR (95% confidence interval [CI]) was 29% (23%-36%) overall (n = 189) and 33% (25%-42%) in second-line treatment (n = 118). Patients with brain metastases had lower ORR (17% vs 32% without; odds ratio, 0.28 [95% CI: 0.10-0.76]). Median (95% CI) PFS and OS were 3.3 (2.6-4.1) and 7.6 (6.4-8.7) months. OS was shorter with platinum-resistant vs platinum-sensitive disease (5.8 vs 9.3 months; hazard ratio, 1.63 [95% CI: 1.17-2.28]). Eighty-eight (33%) patients had treatment-related adverse events, including anemia (8%) and neutropenia (7%); 21 (8%) discontinued treatment due to adverse events.
CONCLUSIONS: In a broad, real-world population with previously treated SCLC, lurbinectedin was associated with clinically meaningful effectiveness and predictable and manageable safety. Lower ORR and OS were seen in patients with brain metastases and platinum-resistant disease, respectively.

title: Protocol for profiling chromatin accessibility in human small-cell lung cancer FFPE-derived samples using Omni-ATAC-seq.
authors: Salataj E, Kawasaki K, Massagué J et al.
abstract: The assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples maps accessible chromatin in archival tissues, but DNA degradation and crosslinking remain significant challenges when processing these samples. Here, we present a protocol for Omni-ATAC-seq on degraded human small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) FFPE-derived samples. We detail steps for successful nuclei isolation, efficient tagmentation, and optimal library amplification to overcome the low signal-to-noise ratio. This protocol enables high-quality epigenetic profiling, turning archived SCLC samples into valuable resources for studying disease progression. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Kawasaki et al.1.

title: Clinical and pathological characteristics, immune microenvironment, and survival analysis of molecular subtypes of surgically resected small cell lung cancer.
authors: Tian J, He J, Tian H et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited therapeutic progress, largely due to its heterogeneity and the lack of biomarkers for patient stratification. This study aims to validate the prevalent molecular subtyping system in a surgically resected cohort and elucidate the subtype-specific tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and its clinical implications.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed the clinical and pathological characteristics of 80 patients with surgically resected SCLC. The expression levels of Achaete-scute family BHLH transcription factor 1 (ASCL1), neuronal differentiation 1 (NEUROD1), POU class 2 homeobox 3 (POU2F3), as well as the immune markers CD8, forkhead box P3 (FOXP3), and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), were assessed in 80 pathological tissue samples using immunohistochemistry (IHC). Statistical analyses, including the chi-square test, t-test, and univariate and multivariate Cox regression, were performed to evaluate the associations between SCLC molecular subtype expression levels and patients' clinicopathological features, immune marker profiles, and prognostic outcomes.
RESULTS: All four molecular subtypes were successfully identified and exhibited distinct distribution patterns: ASCL1-dominant SCLC (SCLC-A, 53.8%), NEUROD1-dominant SCLC (SCLC-N, 5.0%), POU2F3-dominant SCLC (SCLC-P, 3.8%), and SCLC-triple-negative (37.5%). These subtypes were not associated with conventional clinicopathological characteristics. Each subtype displayed unique TIME features. SCLC-A correlated with an immunosuppressive microenvironment enriched in FOXP3 + regulatory T cells (Tregs) (r = 0.458, P < 0.001). SCLC-triple-negative, despite showing higher PD-L1 expression, exhibited an immune-infiltrated phenotype and was positively correlated with CD8 + T cells (r = 0.451, P < 0.001). In contrast, SCLC-N and SCLC-P presented an "immune-desert" phenotype. Furthermore, elevated levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and PD-L1 were identified as independent prognostic risk factors for shorter overall survival (OS), and these molecular subtypes were significantly associated with OS (log-rank P = 0.043).
CONCLUSIONS: This study based on IHC detection, validated the proposed molecular subtyping classification of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) through the expression patterns of transcriptional regulators. The findings demonstrated that SCLC-A and SCLC-triple-negative were respectively associated with distinct tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) features and poorer prognostic outcomes. Furthermore, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) were identified as independent prognostic factors in surgically resected SCLC patients. These conclusions may contribute to treatment decision-making for SCLC.

title: Carcinoids of the lung caused by exogenous noxious agents: a scoping review.
authors: Kilo S, Schröder C, Frei-Stuber L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Approximately 2% of lung tumours are pulmonary carcinoids (PCs), divided into typical (90%) and atypical (AC) (10%). The link with external exposure to carcinogens remains controversial.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between occupational exposure to carcinogens and PC tumours.
METHODS: A PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review was performed. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed and Embase (January 2025). Studies were reviewed, data extracted, analysed and summarised narratively.
RESULTS: 1302 studies were reviewed. 27 original studies and seven conference papers on topics including exposure to cigarette smoke (n=23) and asbestos (n=6), or mechanistic information, were included. Following the collapse of the World Trade Center in 2001, carcinoids accounted for 6% of lung cancer cases in people exposed to the resulting dust (9% in women, 3% in men). The proportion of ACs among carcinoids rose from 9.3% (controls) to 16.3% (smokers) and from ∼25% to 45% (probable versus definite asbestos exposure). Basic research has identified biological pathways linking harmful exposures (such as asbestos and cigarette smoke) to neuroendocrine cell proliferation and the potential progression of PCs to higher-grade lung tumours.
DISCUSSION: The significance these of findings is limited due to 1) the limited number of studies, 2) the small number of tumours within those studies and 3) the lack of rigid diagnostic (morphological and molecular) criteria for PCs in most studies. Nevertheless, a consistent finding is a higher proportion of AC among carcinoids, particularly following asbestos exposure.
CONCLUSIONS: Based on these findings, a link between carcinogenic substances (especially asbestos and cigarette smoke) and carcinoids seems plausible. More stringent analyses in epidemiological surveys are needed to further clarify the pathogenesis of PCs.

title: CREBBP loss drives immune evasion by epigenetically silencing STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer.
authors: Gao Q, Wei K, Pan D et al.
abstract: Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify CREBBP loss, a frequent genetic alteration in SCLC, as a key suppressor of tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses that drives an immune-cold tumor microenvironment in Rb1/Trp53-driven autochthonous mouse models. Consistently, Crebbp deletion promotes immune escape in syngeneic SCLC models. Mechanistically, Crebbp loss suppresses Sting and major histocompatibility complex class-I expression by reducing histone H3 acetylation. Notably, HDAC inhibition restores histone acetylation, reactivates these silenced genes, and induces tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses. Moreover, pharmacological HDAC inhibition synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade to suppress tumor growth in both Crebbp-mutant and Crebbp-wild-type SCLCs, with a more prominent effect in Crebbp-mutant tumors. Collectively, these findings establish CREBBP loss as a key mechanism of immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in SCLC, highlighting HDAC inhibition as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

title: A Phase I Study of HS-20093 in Combination With ZG006 With or Without Adebrelimab in Patients With ES-SCLC
conditions: Extensive Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer (ES-SCLC)
summary: This is a multicenter, open-label Phase I study evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic, and efficacy of Intravenous HS-20093 in combination with ZG006 with or without adebrelimab in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer.

title: Study of radon diffusion coefficient of synthetic and natural fibers for radon mitigation applications.
authors: Prajith R, Rout RP, Mishra R et al.
abstract: As long-term exposure to elevated radon (222Rn) levels has been associated with an increased risk of developing lung cancer, radon mitigation is essential in high radon background areas to decrease the inhalation dose as well as in underground laboratories where 222Rn can be a background for high-energy physics experiments. In this regard, the generally used radon mitigation strategies comprise of soil depressurization, sealing the emanating surfaces, using barriers and membranes, providing appropriate ventilation etc. In the present study a dual chamber diffusion sampler based on ISO/TS 11665-13:2017 was developed to test the radon mitigation factors of commercially available synthetic and natural fibers. Radon diffusion coefficient in these barrier materials was also determined. Use of natural fibers for radon mitigation will form a database of eco-friendly barrier materials for sustainable mitigation of radon.

title: Associations of hematological and biochemical parameters with radon exposure among male miners in China.
authors: Guo X, Gao G, Ruan J et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Radon is a radioactive gas that produces a large amount of alpha particles during its decay process and a well-recognized health hazard, particularly an established risk factor for lung cancer in high-risk populations such as miners. Although hematological and biochemical parameters are useful indicators of human health status, the impact of radon exposure on these parameters among male miners remains unclear.
METHODS: The participants of this study are 283 male miners in a tin mine in China. A targeted research design was adopted to conduct a questionnaire survey, physical examination, blood sample analysis coupled with radon concentration measurements, statistical analysis was performed to investigate the impact of varying levels of radon exposure on hematological and biochemical parameters among the participants.
RESULTS: Mean platelet volume (MPV), plateletcrit (PCT), and platelet-large cell ratio (P-LCR) decreased significantly across the working-level month (WLM) groups (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.003), as did albumin (ALB) and the albumin-to-globulin (A/G) ratio (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045). In contrast, urea and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased significantly (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045), whereas platelet count did not differ significantly among groups. Multiple linear regression confirmed WLM as an independent predictor for MPV (β= -0.282, P < 0.0001), PCT (β= -0.165, P = 0.010), P-LCR (β= -0.206, P = 0.002), urea (β = 0.178, P = 0.008), and platelet distribution width (β = 0.184, P = 0.006). All values remained within clinically normal reference ranges.
CONCLUSION: Cumulative occupational radon exposure was independently associated with decreased platelet volume indices and elevated urea levels in miners, suggesting subclinical hematological changes and altered renal-related parameters. MPV may serve as a candidate indicator requiring further validation of radiation-related hematopoietic alterations. These findings contribute to occupational health surveillance frameworks for populations chronically exposed to radon in mining environments.

title: CT low attenuation area quantification versus visual scoring for early pulmonary emphysema detection in lung cancer screening.
authors: Liu H, Han D, Heuvelmans MA et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare low-attenuation analysis (LAA) with visual scoring and explore their application in the detection of emphysema in low-dose CT (LDCT) scans.
METHODS: A random cohort of 352 CT examinations from health-check participants was selected from a lung cancer screening(LCS) dataset. Scans were evaluated for emphysema by four readers according to latest Fleischner criteria, and emphysema was quantified by LAA with thresholds from -900 HU to -980 HU. Fleiss' Kappa assessed inter-reader agreement on visual detection and severity classification. Cases with full agreement on emphysema presence were used to compare LAA quantification and visual detection. Spearman correlation test measured their correlation and Cohen's Kappa evaluated the agreement between LAA%-measured emphysema and visual detection.
RESULTS: Agreement among four observers was found in 266 cases on emphysema presence based on visual evaluation (K = 0.738, 0.737-0.739). Concordance between emphysema presence using a LAA% cutoff of 6% and binary visual classification was 61.3% (163/266, Cohen's Kappa:0.173. Spearman analysis showed a correlation between LAA% and visual scores (P < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: LAA emphysema quantification shows in comparison with visual scoring limited performance for discrimination of normal and emphysematous lung parenchyma in a Low dose CT Lung cancer screening dataset.
ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Full agreement among four readers regarding visual emphysema classification was achieved in only three-quarters of cases. Limited concordance was found between LAA%-measured emphysema and visual detection.

title: ACR lung-RADS: updates and future directions.
authors: Petranović M, Prosper AE, Hunsaker AR et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and low-dose CT (LDCT) screening has been shown to significantly reduce lung cancer deaths in high-risk populations. The American College of Radiology (ACR) introduced the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) in 2014 to standardize the reporting and management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules. Since its inception, Lung-RADS has undergone iterative updates reflecting advances in evidence, clinical practice, and the expanding scope of lung cancer screening. This review summarizes the major updates to Lung-RADS, highlights areas of active discussion within the Lung-RADS Committee, and outlines future research directions. Key topics include the ongoing evaluation of volumetric versus diameter-based nodule measurement, the management of subsolid nodules and the balance between surveillance and intervention, the implementation of Category 0 for infectious or inflammatory findings, clarification of juxtapleural nodule classification, the approach to incidental findings, and the development of a Lung-RADS Atlas. Future directions address the integration of risk-based and category-based assessment approaches, the role of artificial intelligence and deep learning in nodule stratification, the potential incorporation of incidental nodules into Lung-RADS, and the prospect of international harmonization for lung cancer screening reporting and management. Lung-RADS has become an essential reporting and quality tool for lung cancer screening in the United States and increasingly worldwide. Continued refinement, guided by emerging evidence, multidisciplinary collaboration, and technological innovation, will be critical to advancing precision screening strategies and reducing the global burden of lung cancer.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.
