title: Full-Cohort Organ Dose Assessment from Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening in the National Lung Screening Trial.
authors: Lee C, Moroz B, Hwang EJ et al.
abstract:
RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Organ-specific dose estimates are needed to characterize radiation exposure from repeated low-dose computed tomography (CT) lung cancer screening in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). The objective was to estimate study-level doses and participant-level cumulative doses in the NLST CT screening cohort.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective dosimetry study included 25,051 NLST CT screening participants from the Lung Screening Study and American College of Radiology Imaging Network components after excluding participants with any examination lacking a valid manufacturer-appropriate tube current-time input. Image-series metadata were linked with age, sex, height, and weight, and then valid records were grouped into 69,601 study-level screening examinations. Organ absorbed doses and effective dose were calculated using the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for Computed Tomography with sex- and body-size-specific adult phantoms. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was assessed with 50 stochastic simulations.
RESULTS: Participants underwent a mean of 2.78 study-level screening examinations; the median study-level volume CT dose index was 3.30 mGy. Median (interquartile range) study-level lung, breast, heart wall, active marrow, and effective doses were 3.93 (3.13-4.96), 3.94 (3.14-5.04), 3.94 (3.14-5.01), and 1.26 (0.99-1.60) mGy, and 2.07 (1.65-2.59) mSv, respectively. Corresponding cumulative participant-level doses were 11.30 (8.89-14.50), 11.39 (9.01-14.75), 11.41 (8.93-14.66), and 3.63 (2.79-4.66) mGy, and 5.94 (4.69-7.64) mSv. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was greatest for thyroid dose (mean coefficient of variation, 21.1%) and low for in-field organs.
CONCLUSION: Using NLST low-dose CT screening data, we estimated participant-level cumulative organ and effective doses and characterized variation across organs and body-size groups.

title: Carbon nanoparticle exposure promotes the progression of non-small cell lung cancer via the ARNT2/ARL14 axis: Findings from in vivo and in vitro models.
authors: Jiang W, Lu C, Yang Y et al.
abstract: We investigated whether carbon nanoparticles (CNPs), a shared core component of coal dust, ambient PM2.5, and tobacco smoke, drive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) progression. In an experimental mouse model of CNP‑induced pulmonary fibrosis (intranasal instillation, 200 µg/kg every other day for 90 days), we used transcriptomic screening to identify aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator 2 (ARNT2) as a key upregulated transcription factor. In an ectopic xenograft model (nude mice pre‑exposed to 15 µg/kg CNPs for 1 week, subsequently inoculated with A549/A427 cells with or without ARNT2 silencing, with CNP administration continued for a total of 40 days), CNP exposure increased tumor volume at day 36 (A549, 194 ± 17-308 ± 22 mm³; A427, 245 ± 31-417 ± 42 mm³), proliferation (Ki‑67/PCNA: A549, 2.93‑/3.33-fold; A427, 1.94‑/3.55-fold), and levels of epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers (N‑cadherin/Vimentin: A549, 1.61‑/3.17-fold; A427, 2.44‑/1.98-fold), while ARNT2 knockdown reversed these effects. In vitro, CNP treatment (2 µg/mL, 48 h) enhanced proliferation (A549, 2.01‑fold; A427, 1.43-fold), migration (A549, 1.83‑fold; A427, 3.61‑fold), invasion (A549, 2.50‑fold; A427, 2.40‑fold), levels of stemness markers (CD133/SOX2/Oct4: A549, 2.38-/1.93-/2.02-fold; A427, 2.44-/1.44-/1.60-fold), and concentrations of inflammatory cytokines (TNF‑α/IL‑1β/IL‑6: A549, 5.39‑/6.41-/13.70-fold; A427, 3.59‑/10.02-/9.66-fold), reduced apoptosis (A549, 0.47‑fold; A427, 0.36-fold) and senescence (A549, 0.61-fold; A427, 0.37-fold), and increased reactive oxygen species levels (A549, 2.32‑fold; A427, 2.01‑fold); all these changes were attenuated by ARNT2 silencing. Transcriptomic and bioinformatic analyses identified ADP-ribosylation factor-like protein 14 (ARL14) as a downstream effector of ARNT2; ARL14 overexpression in ARNT2‑silenced cells restored proliferation and invasion and reduced apoptosis. Overall, experimental CNP exposure promotes NSCLC progression in an ARNT2-dependent manner, with ARL14 as a downstream mediator, which suggests potential targets for intervention in particulate-associated lung cancer.

title: From discovery to clinical implementation: a bibliometric analysis of DNA methylation biomarkers in non-small cell lung cancer, 1999-2025.
authors: Li Y, Wu F, Liu W et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: DNA methylation alterations are stable, biologically informative, and detectable in tissue and circulating DNA, making them promising biomarkers for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, few methylation biomarkers have entered routine clinical practice. We aimed to characterize the evolution and translational challenges of this field.
METHODS: Publications on NSCLC, DNA methylation, and biomarker applications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection through 31 December 2025. After PRISMA-based screening, bibliometric and knowledge-map analyses were performed.
RESULTS: A total of 1,910 publications were included. Annual output increased after 2010 and peaked in 2022. Lung Cancer was the most productive journal, whereas Cancer Research had the highest citation impact. China contributed the largest publication volume, while the United States had the highest citation impact. Foundational studies focused on promoter hypermethylation, methylation-specific PCR, and methylated DNA detection in accessible biospecimens. Research priorities shifted from candidate-gene studies toward methylation signatures, liquid biopsy, multi-omics integration, immunotherapy-related applications, and computational modeling.
CONCLUSION: NSCLC methylation biomarker research has evolved toward integrated translational frameworks. Future progress requires multicenter validation, standardized platforms, clinically defined methylation panels, and AI-assisted integration.
PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero identifier is CRD420261426546.

title: Clinical characteristics and prognostic analysis of patients with connective tissue disease complicated by non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Zhang G, Ding Q, Zhang L et al.
abstract:
AIMS: To summarize the clinical features, treatment patterns and survival outcomes of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) combined with connective tissue disease (CTD), and to determine whether CTD independently influences prognosis and treatment-related toxicity in this special patient population.
METHODS: In this retrospective study, we enrolled 200 consecutive patients with pathologically confirmed NSCLC. Among them, 95 patients met the diagnostic criteria for CTD were set as the CTD group, and the remaining 105 patients with simple NSCLC as the control group. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), baseline tumor characteristics, metastatic patterns, first-line treatment patterns and delivery, and treatment-related adverse events (AEs). We adopted Kaplan-Meier method for survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression model for prognostic analysis. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the prognostic effect of CTD and identify independent survival predictors.
RESULTS: The CTD group presented more severe intrathoracic tumor dissemination, including higher incidence of bilateral pulmonary lesions (P = 0.042) and pleural effusion (P = 0.011). Compared with controls, the CTD group were less likely to receive platinum-based doublet chemotherapy (P = 0.035), cisplatin-based chemotherapy (P = 0.017), immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-containing therapy (P = 0.009) and thoracic radiotherapy (P = 0.029). Meanwhile, the CTD group had higher risks of chemotherapy dose reduction (P = 0.011), treatment delay longer than 7 days (P = 0.015) and early treatment discontinuation (P = 0.002). In survival outcomes, the median PFS was 5.4 vs 7.8 months (HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.17-2.13; P = 0.003), and the median OS was 9.7 vs 14.6 months (HR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.29-2.40; P<0.001). The incidence of grade 3-4 treatment-related AEs was significantly higher in the CTD group (P = 0.010). Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that CTD was an independent adverse prognostic factor for poor OS (HR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.01-1.97; P = 0.044).
CONCLUSION: For patients diagnosed with NSCLC, comorbid CTD is correlated with aggravated intrathoracic tumor dissemination, reduced treatment intensity and treatment tolerance, increased severe toxicity, and dismal long-term survival.

title: Relevance between patients' clinical factors and 4D-CT lung ventilation heterogeneity for evaluating the adoption of functional avoidance thoracic radiotherapy with a large patient database.
authors: Deng G, Ying Y, Wang X et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Four-dimensional computed tomography (4D-CT)-guided functional-avoidance radiotherapy reduces radiation pneumonitis, but the lack of patient selection criteria limits its adoption. This study aimed to identify clinical predictors of lung ventilation heterogeneity and determine which patients derive the greatest dosimetric benefit from functional-avoidance planning.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 274 lung cancer patients. 4D-CT ventilation imaging was generated via deformable registration and a density-change algorithm, and the coefficient of variation (CoV) across six lung zones quantified heterogeneity. Clinical factors were assessed using Mann-Whitney U, Spearman, and multivariable logistic regression for three ventilation outcomes. Thirty-two patients were selected from CoV quartiles and re-planned with functional-avoidance plans; dosimetric parameters were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction applied to address multiple comparisons.
RESULTS: Univariate analysis showed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and airway obstruction reduced bilateral mean ventilation, while central tumors impaired ipsilateral ventilation. Higher CoV was observed in stage III-IV versus I-II, central versus peripheral tumors, and patients with airway obstruction. Multivariable analysis identified airway obstruction as an independent predictor of elevated CoV (adjusted OR = 2.914, 95% CI: 1.315-6.454, P<0.05). Central location and advanced stage showed borderline significance, while COPD trended toward lower CoV. Dosimetrically, functional-avoidance plans reduced functional lung metrics in a heterogeneity-dependent manner. After FDR correction, key metrics (fMLD, fV10, fV20, fV30) remained significant in Group 1 (highest CoV; Q = 0.040-0.049), while significance diminished in lower CoV groups. Leave-one-out (LOO) sensitivity analysis confirmed fMLD and fV20 as robust endpoints. Furthermore, beam arrangement modifications were most frequent in Group 1 (5/8 patients) and absent in Group 4 (0/8), reflecting clinical optimization needs rather than confounding.
CONCLUSIONS: Ventilation heterogeneity is driven by tumor burden and airway patency. Patients with advanced stage, central tumors, or airway obstruction exhibit the strongest heterogeneity and may represent appropriate candidates for functional-avoidance radiotherapy in future prospective trials. However, as this replanning study lacked clinical follow-up for radiation pneumonitis, these findings reflect dosimetric rather than confirmed clinical patient-level benefit. Notably, CoV quartiles were derived from internal median splits within this cohort and require external validation. This study provides a dosimetric basis for hypothesis-generating patient selection.

title: Utility and Safety of a Novel Preoperative Marking via Ultrathin Bronchoscopy in Thoracic Surgery.
authors: Kimura H, Ito T, Nakamura S et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Virtual-assisted lung mapping (VAL-MAP) is a safe and useful procedure for identifying suitable lines for sublobar lung resections. Nonetheless, the current VAL-MAP technique using a thin bronchoscope limits access to peripheral lung regions, including the upper lobes or the S6 region.
METHODS: To overcome this limitation, we developed a new technique utilizing an ultrathin bronchoscope (UTB), termed 'UTB VAL-MAP', enabling precise dye marking of the visceral pleura which is difficult to access with a thin bronchoscope. We retrospectively evaluated the efficacy and safety of UTB VAL-MAP with those of conventional VAL-MAP at our institution.
RESULTS: Overall, 178 preoperative markings (75 patients) were included: 74 markings in 35 patients in the UTB VAL-MAP group and 104 markings in 40 patients in the conventional VAL-MAP group. The overall detection rate in the UTB VAL-MAP group was significantly higher than that in the conventional VAL-MAP group [97.3% (72/74) vs. 84.6% (88/104); P = 0.005]. Furthermore, the marking success rate using indigo carmine in the UTB VAL-MAP group was higher for lesions located in the upper lobe and S6 region than that in the conventional VAL-MAP group (P < 0.001). In multivariate generalized estimating equations models, UTB use (odds ratio = 7.390, P = 0.015) was significantly associated with overall detection rate. No severe procedure-related complications occurred in either group.
CONCLUSION: UTB VAL-MAP appears useful for increasing the rate of successful visceral pleura marking, particularly in the upper lobes or S6 areas, which the conventional VAL-MAP technique has difficulty reaching, without increasing complications.

title: Quality assessment of synthetic data in healthcare: a critical appraisal with a focus on subgroup bias.
authors: Chatzichristos C, Katsimpokis D, Lai C et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The creation of synthetic data in healthcare research has emerged as a compelling solution to address challenges related to data privacy, in case of data-sharing and data scarceness for training machine learning models.
OBJECTIVE: The current paper aims to provide a critical landscape analysis of synthetic data quality metrics used in healthcare, mapping the state of the field, examining how current fidelity and utility scores often fail to capture weaknesses that appear in specific patient subgroups, and illustrating these blind spots with a lung-cancer case study. We specifically set out to highlight the need for assessing synthetic datasets not only at the aggregate level but also across clinically meaningful subgroups, to ensure reliability and fairness in downstream applications.
METHODS: By examining the landscape of synthetic data adoption in healthcare, we highlight the methodological and utility considerations that shape its integration into the research ecosystem. We elucidate how synthetic data can expedite research initiatives, support data-driven decision-making, and facilitate innovative methodologies while safeguarding sensitive patient information. Conversely, while many papers focus solely on the advantages of synthetic data, we aim to highlight also the potential constraints of using synthetic data in a real-world case involving lung cancer patient level data. Our analysis centers on identifying situations where synthetic data might introduce biases or inaccuracies that hinder the generation of meaningful clinical insights.
RESULTS: We demonstrate the limitations of using synthetic data in a lung cancer case study, especially when dealing with small subgroups from the original dataset. While high values for fidelity and utility metrics are achieved when considering the entire synthetic dataset, significant discrepancies arise in cross-classification performance when examining subsets. Additionally, visual inspection reveals spurious correlations in the synthetic data that are not present in the real data.
CONCLUSION: Global realism scores can give a false sense of security: in our case study, metrics that rate the full dataset as "high quality" overlook errors which appear once we zoom in on specific subgroups. We argue that future work must (i) design subgroup-aware fidelity and utility metrics, (ii) favor conditional generators that model rare strata explicitly, and (iii) report metric panels alongside qualitative, clinical sanity checks. Until such standards mature, our analysis highlights that researchers and regulators should treat synthetic data with caution.

title: Diagnostic challenges in WHO classification of thymic epithelial tumors: The clinical value of an international expert pathology panel.
authors: Dimmers MM, Dumoulin DW, den Bakker MA et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) are rare mediastinal tumors classified according to the WHO classification system. Classification can be challenging due to overlapping histological features. Subtyping on biopsy specimens is often inaccurate due to tumor heterogeneity and sampling effect. Since 2012 an international thymic tumor pathology expert panel is available in the Netherlands. This study evaluates the added value of this panel by assessing the discrepancies in diagnosis, inter-observer agreement and concordance on diagnosis between biopsy and the subsequent resection specimen.
METHODS: All pathology excerpts from 2012 until 2024 for patients diagnosed with a thymic tumor were extracted from the national PALGA database and evaluated for histological subtype, assessment and the thymoma panel result.
RESULTS: In total 1163 resection and 304 biopsy specimens were included, of which 36.1% were submitted to the thymoma panel. The diagnosis changed in 15.7% of cases after assessment. The subtypes AB and Bmix were most often submitted to the thymoma panel and the diagnosis changed most often for subtype A, B3 or Bmix. In 72.8% the concordance between the panel members exceeded 90%. The biopsy diagnosis varied from the resection diagnosis in 46.8%, but the differentiation between thymoma and thymic carcinoma was accurate on biopsy.
CONCLUSION: A panel of dedicated pathologists with experience in thymic abnormalities contributed substantially to a more accurate classification of TETs, thereby guiding optimal treatment planning and prognostic evaluation. Despite the discrepancies between biopsy and resection specimens, distinguishing thymoma from thymic carcinoma was accurate on biopsy.

title: Implantable Microdevices for in Situ Evaluation of Drug Responses in Lung Cancer
summary:
This research is being done to study the safety and feasibility of implanting and retrieving a microdevice that releases microdoses of 20 specific drugs or drug combinations as a possible tool to evaluate the effectiveness of several cancer drugs against lung cancer or mesothelioma.

The name of the intervention(s) involved in this study are:

Implantable Microdevice (IMD) Surgery (excision of tumor) Drugs used in this study will include drugs already used as standard of care for the treatment of lung cancer and mesothelioma, or other drugs that are approved or being investigated for these indications.

title: First-line Treatment With Dual Immunotherapy Combined With Anti-angiogenesis for Unresectable Advanced Malignant Peritoneal Mesothelioma
summary: This is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm, Phase II clinical study evaluating the efficacy and safety of sintilimab in combination with ipilimumab N01 and bevacizumab as first-line treatment in patients with unresectable malignant peritoneal mesothelioma. Eligible patients will receive sintilimab plus ipilimumab N01 and bevacizumab until disease progression, death, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of informed consent, initiation of a new anti-tumor therapy, or other protocol-defined reasons, with a maximum treatment duration of 24 months. The primary endpoint is progression-free survival (PFS).

title: Recurrent leukaemia stem cell states define the antigenic landscape of paediatric Acute Myeloid Leukaemia
summary: Paediatric acute myeloid leukaemia (pAML) remains a leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, with disease heterogeneity representing a major obstacle to effective immunotherapy. To enable rational immunotherapy design accounting for such heterogeneity, we combined single-cell transcriptomics and surface proteomics (CITE-seq). Using an integrated framework for malignant cell identification and unbiased gene program identification, we resolved three conserved leukaemia stem cell (LSC) subtypes, primitive (P-LSC), monocytic (M-LSC), and erythroid-like (E-LSC), that frequently coexist within individual patients in varying proportions and represent distinct stem-cell states with characteristic immunophenotypes and transcriptional programmes. Quantitative surface antigen profiling revealed that no single target achieved full LSC coverage. CLEC12A, an antigen currently being evaluated clinically, was expressed across P-LSC and M-LSC but was largely absent from E-LSC. In contrast, CD84 provided complementary coverage in the P and M groups and served as the primary target in the E-LSC population. The combination of CLEC12A and CD84 provided broad coverage across all three LSC subtypes, while sparing healthy haematopoietic stem cells. Validation across independent single-cell and bulk cohorts confirmed the robustness of this combination. These findings establish a paediatric-specific framework for antigen prioritisation in AML, identify CLEC12A/CD84 as a robust dual-targeting strategy across heterogeneous LSC states, and provide a blueprint for the rational design of next-generation CAR T-cell combinations.

title: Pan-pediatric brain tumor microRNA networks define immune microenvironment states and responses to CAR T-cell therapy
summary: Pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, yet molecular programs that shape their immune microenvironments and response to immunotherapy remain poorly defined. Because microRNAs (miRNAs) coordinately regulate gene expression across multiple pathways, we hypothesized that miRNA programs may capture broader immune states than individual immune-regulatory molecules. We integrated small RNA and bulk transcriptomic profiles from diffuse midline glioma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma, and low-grade glioma to identify miRNA programs associated with tumor immune states. Across tumor histologies, dysregulated miRNAs were associated with T-cell, natural killer cell, antigen-presentation, and myeloid programs. Diffuse midline glioma exhibited a distinct miRNA program associated with reduced lymphocyte signatures and increased suppressive myeloid features. Longitudinal profiling of immunocompetent glioma models during B7-H3 CAR T-cell therapy revealed dynamic remodeling of miRNA and immune transcriptional programs. Human tumor-associated miRNAs were significantly enriched among miRNAs associated with CAR T response in vivo. Functional interrogation of miR-149 demonstrated enhanced CAR T-cell expansion and sustained antitumor activity during repeated antigen stimulation. Together, these data define miRNA programs associated with immune states across pediatric CNS tumors and identify miR-149 as a candidate regulator of CAR T-cell function, providing a genomic framework for developing miRNA-directed strategies to improve CAR T-cell therapy.
